newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to approve Boeing merger on Wednesday.
newsitem.headline: EU to approve Boeing merger on Wednesday.

text.p: The European Commission will on Wednesday formally approve the merger of Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp., European Union sources said Tuesday.
"I don't anticipate any problems at all," one source said.
The decision is seen as a formality after the EU's advisory committee of national competition experts last Friday approved the $15 billion deal.
Only one representative in the committee, which has only an advisory role, expressed reservations.
The European Commission gave its preliminary blessing after Boeing agreed to a number of last-minute concessions aimed at reducing the deal's anti-competitive effect in Europe.

However, European research chief Edith Cresson, one of two French members of the Commission, said she disagreed with the preliminary ruling, arguing that the concessions would not prevent Boeing from acquiring a near or total monopoly in some markets.
An EU source said Cresson still had reservations but that there would probably not be a vote at Wednesday's meeting.
In case of a vote, a simple majority would be enough for the 20-member Commission to approve the deal.
The merger, which was announced in December, brings together Boeing's commanding role in the commercial aviation sector and McDonnell Douglas' expertise in manufacturing military aircraft.
Boeing's share of the commercial jet market will increase to 70 percent from its current level of 64 percent, leaving only the European consortium Airbus in a position to compete.

The merged company is expected to generate $49 billion in revenue this year, of which 61 percent would come from commercial jets. Without the acquisition, Boeing would have $34.7 billion in revenue this year, with 76 percent coming from the commercial side.

To win EU approval, the Seattle-based company has pledged not to enforce exclusivity provisions in its long-term supply contracts with AMR Corp.'s American Airlines, Continental Airlines and Delta Airlines.
It also agreed not to conclude any new exclusive aircraft supply contracts with airlines before Aug. 1, 2007, after the Commission threatened to block the deal.
The last-minute concessions averted the threat of a transatlantic trade dispute.
